title: First English Witchcraft Act: Henry VIII Makes Witchcraft a Capital Felony
description: The Witchcraft Act of 1542, passed under Henry VIII, was the first English statute specifically making witchcraft a capital felony rather than an ecclesiastical offense. The act targeted conjurations, witchcraft, and sorcery performed for purposes including treasure-finding, provoking unlawful love, destroying persons or property, or 'wasting, consuming, or destroying' persons. The act was repealed in 1547 under Edward VI, partly because Henry's advisers had used witchcraft accusations against political opponents, making Parliament wary of the statute's abuse potential. This brief first act established the principle of secular criminal jurisdiction over witchcraft that would be elaborated in the 1563 and 1604 acts.
historiographical_note: James Sharpe's Instruments of Darkness: Witchcraft in England 1550–1750 (1996) provides context for the 1542 act within the development of English witchcraft law. The act's quick repeal is significant: it shows that Parliament was aware of the statute's political abuse potential — a concern that would shape the more carefully drafted 1563 act.
source_method: 33 Henry VIII c.8 (1542); secondary scholarship on English witchcraft legislation
